title: Feelings Are Weather and Temperature
why: English speakers constantly describe emotions and relationships as temperature and weather: a warm welcome, a frosty silence, a stormy marriage. Recognising the system helps you read tone instantly and pick the right register.
know: eight core weather and temperature idioms, such as break the ice and steal someone's thunder
understand: that warmth usually means friendliness, while cold means distance, hostility or nervousness
that storms stand for conflict and sudden emotion, and calm stands for control
able: choose the right weather idiom for a social or work situation
vary these idioms naturally without breaking them
discuss songs, poems and plays that turn weather into feeling
mistakes: I have cold legs about the wedding.
I'm getting cold feet about the wedding. Always feet, usually with get or have.
Let's cut the ice with a quick game.
Let's break the ice with a quick game. The verb is fixed.
It was just a storm in a glass of water.
It was just a storm in a teacup. The glass of water is a literal translation; Americans say a tempest in a teapot.
I'm under the weather; I broke my leg skiing.
Under the weather means mildly ill, not injured: just say I broke my leg skiing.
(Formal letter) Regrettably, I must take a rain check on your kind invitation.
Regrettably, I am unable to attend. Take a rain check is casual and North American.
bigidea: In English, emotional closeness is temperature. Friendly people are warm, distant people are cool or cold, and anger heats up. Linguists link this to early bodily experience: being held close is being kept warm.
Moods are weather: a sunny disposition, a cloud hanging over someone, a storm of protest. Weather happens to us, so this metaphor often presents feelings as forces we cannot fully control.
Storms also come with a timeline: tension builds, the storm breaks, the air clears. That is why we speak of the calm before the storm or say that an argument cleared the air.
hidden: She gave me an icy stare across the boardroom.
Relations between the two countries have cooled since the election.
He has a sunny personality, even on Monday mornings.
A cloud hung over the team after the layoffs.
The minister faced a storm of criticism.
Let's talk it through and clear the air.

expressions.meaning: say or do something to ease tension when people first meet
expressions.example: Our trainer broke the ice by asking everyone about the worst job they'd ever had.
expressions.bend: Flexible in tense and as a noun: an icebreaker, a good ice-breaking question. Keep break and ice.
expressions.note: Shakespeare used it in The Taming of the Shrew (early 1590s), helping to make it popular. The image is a ship cutting through frozen water to open a route.

expressions.meaning: become nervous and hesitate about something you planned or promised to do
expressions.example: Two days before signing the lease, Marco got cold feet and asked for another week.
expressions.bend: Works with get, have or develop, and as a noun: a case of cold feet. Feet stays plural.
expressions.note: Strongly linked to weddings. The near-synonym have second thoughts is milder and more neutral.

expressions.meaning: take attention or praise away from someone, often by doing or saying their thing first
expressions.example: I was about to share my news, but my sister stole my thunder by announcing her engagement over dessert.
expressions.bend: The possessive changes freely: steal her thunder, stole the CEO's thunder. Never lightning.
expressions.note: From the critic and playwright John Dennis, who devised a new thunder effect for his play Appius and Virginia (1709). When a rival theatre reused it, he complained they had stolen his thunder.

expressions.meaning: a lot of anger or worry about something unimportant
expressions.example: The row over the office fridge rota turned out to be a storm in a teacup.
expressions.bend: British and Canadian form; Americans usually say a tempest in a teapot. Don't mix the two halves.
expressions.note: Calling someone else's concern a storm in a teacup can sound dismissive, so be careful using it about another person's worries.

expressions.meaning: a quiet period just before trouble or intense activity
expressions.example: The office was strangely silent on Sunday night, the calm before the storm of the year-end audit.
expressions.bend: Often framed as this is just the calm before the storm. Writers sometimes reverse it, the storm before the calm, for effect.
expressions.note: Used half-jokingly about busy seasons at work, but also seriously in news reports about conflict or extreme weather.

expressions.example: I'm a bit under the weather, so I'll join the meeting by video.
expressions.bend: Mostly fixed. Soften or intensify before it: a bit, slightly, feeling under the weather.
expressions.note: A polite, vague way to explain an absence. Using it about a serious illness or a hospital stay sounds oddly understated.

expressions.meaning: an unfriendly, cold response from people
expressions.example: The new parking fees got a frosty reception from local shop owners.
expressions.bend: Both words bend: a chilly reception, a frosty response, the atmosphere was frosty.
expressions.note: Common in journalism and business reporting. The opposite is a warm welcome, not a hot reception.

expressions.meaning: politely decline an invitation while suggesting another time
expressions.example: I'll have to take a rain check on drinks tonight; how about Thursday?
expressions.bend: Also Can I take a rain check? or simply Rain check? Usually two words; raincheck also appears.
expressions.note: North American, from baseball tickets that let fans return if a game was rained out. British speakers understand it but may say another time.

culture.how: In Act 3 the old king, rejected by his daughters, wanders across a heath in a violent storm. The wild weather outside mirrors the chaos in his mind and in his kingdom, a classic example of weather standing in for feeling.
culture.ask: Can you think of a film or novel where the weather matches a character's emotions? Does it work, or is it a cliche?

culture.how: A tiny poem that compares fog to a cat: it arrives silently, sits looking over the city and harbour, then moves on. Here the metaphor runs the other way, giving weather the quiet, independent mood of an animal.
culture.ask: What animal would you compare a thunderstorm or a heatwave to, and why?

culture.how: Harrison wrote it on a spring day after a long English winter and a stressful run of business meetings. The returning sun stands for relief and hope: the mood lifts the way the weather lifts.
culture.ask: Does a particular season or kind of weather change your mood? Describe it with a metaphor.
culture.find: The Beatles Here Comes the Sun

culture.by: Johnny Cash (written by June Carter and Merle Kilgore)
culture.how: The song describes falling in love as falling into fire. Passion is heat: exciting and irresistible, but also painful and dangerous. It shows how far the temperature metaphor can stretch, from warm affection to burning desire.
culture.ask: Is love more often warm or hot in the songs you know? What's the difference?

culture.how: The singer promises to shelter someone through bad weather. Rain stands for hard times and the umbrella for loyalty and protection, turning a simple object into a symbol of a relationship.
culture.ask: Who has been an umbrella for you in hard times? What everyday object would you choose as a symbol of loyalty?

match.r: ease tension when people first meet
match.why: Like a ship breaking frozen water, you open the way for conversation.
Cold means fear here: you lose the courage to go ahead with a plan.

match.r: take attention meant for someone else
match.why: Thunder is the big dramatic effect; stealing it means grabbing someone's moment.
A storm is anger; the teacup shows how small the real issue is.
Weather often goes still just before a storm breaks.
A vague, polite way to say you feel unwell.
Frost is cold, and cold means distant or hostile.
From baseball tickets for rained-out games: you'll come another day.

sort.h: What feeling does each expression suggest? Sort it into warm, cold or stormy.

items.why: A person or thing that brings happiness.
Cold here means nervous and hesitant.
A silence full of disapproval or hostility.
Heat that has become anger: an argument.
A sudden, strong public reaction against something.
It is quiet, but trouble is coming.

pick.q: Nobody spoke at the start of the workshop, so the facilitator asked a silly question to ___.
pick.why: Break the ice: ease the awkward silence at a first meeting.

pick.q: Jun had agreed to run the marathon, but the night before he ___ and stayed home.
pick.why: Got cold feet: lost his nerve at the last minute.

pick.q: Everyone was furious about the new logo for a day and then forgot it; it was ___.
pick.why: A storm in a teacup: a big fuss over something minor.

pick.q: I'd love to come to the barbecue, but I'm swamped this week; can I ___?
pick.why: Take a rain check: decline politely and suggest another time.

pick.q: The intern presented my idea to the boss before I could and completely ___.
pick.why: Stole my thunder: took the credit and attention I expected.

pick.q: The streets are quiet now, but this is just ___: the hurricane arrives tomorrow.
pick.why: The calm before the storm: quiet just before trouble.

pick.q: The mayor's plan to close the library got ___ at the town hall meeting.
pick.why: A frosty reception: people reacted coldly and with disapproval.

pick.q: Grandad is ___ with a cold, so we've postponed our visit until next weekend.
pick.why: Under the weather: mildly ill, perfect for a cold.

spot.q: After two years apart, the reunion was awkward until Dad cracked the ice with a terrible joke.
spot.why: The idiom is fixed: break the ice. Cracked and smashed are not used.

spot.q: She had cold toes about moving to Calgary and nearly turned down the job.
spot.why: Always cold feet: had cold feet or got cold feet about something.

spot.q: Honestly, the argument over the seating plan is a storm in a coffee cup; let it go.
spot.bad: a storm in a coffee cup
opts: a tempest in a coffee cup
spot.why: British and Canadian English: a storm in a teacup. The container is fixed.

spot.q: My colleague stole my lightning by sharing the sales figures before my presentation.
spot.why: Steal someone's thunder comes from a theatre sound effect: thunder, never lightning.

spot.q: I'm feeling under the climate today, so I'll work from home.
spot.why: The fixed phrase is under the weather: slightly ill.

type.q: Both negotiators kept ___ heads while protesters shouted outside the building.
type.why: Keep a cool head: stay calm under pressure. Cool means controlled here.

type.q: The debate on immigration grew so ___ that the moderator called a short break.
type.why: A heated debate is angry and emotional; heat stands for anger.

type.q: Thanks for the invitation; I'll take a rain ___ and call you next week.
type.why: Take a rain check: decline for now. Rain cheque is a Canadian spelling also seen.

type.q: Don't relax yet; this quiet week is just the calm before the ___.
type.why: The calm before the storm: quiet before a busy or difficult time.

type.q: Lena couldn't decide whether to marry Tom, and her family worried she was getting cold ___.
type.why: Get cold feet: become nervous about a commitment, especially a wedding.

type.q: Our team leader asked everyone to share a holiday photo to break the ___ on the first video call.
type.why: Break the ice: ease tension when people first meet.

opts: Her surprise announcement completely stole the CEO's thunder.
Her surprise announcement completely stole the CEO's lightning.
Her surprise announcement completely stole the CEO's thunders.
bend.why: The possessive can change, but thunder stays singular and never becomes lightning.

opts: That quiz brilliantly broke the ices.
That quiz was a brilliant icebreaker.
That quiz was a brilliant ice-cracker.
bend.why: The idiom has a natural noun form: an icebreaker (also ice-breaker).

opts: The proposal met with a decidedly hot reception.
The proposal met with a decidedly snowy reception.
The proposal met with a decidedly chilly reception.
bend.why: Frosty can become chilly or icy, but hot and snowy break the cold-means-unfriendly logic.

opts: He's having serious cold legs about the move.
He's having a serious case of cold foot about the move.
He's having a serious case of cold feet about the move.
bend.why: A case of cold feet is a common, natural variation. Feet stays plural.

talk: Describe a time you got cold feet or had second thoughts. What did you decide in the end?
Role-play: Bill invites you to a dinner party you can't attend. Take a rain check casually, then decline the same invitation in a polite, formal email style.
Think of the storm in King Lear. Why do writers so often make the weather match a character's feelings? Is it effective or a cliche?
What's a good way to break the ice in your culture at a business meeting or a family gathering?
Describe a news story that caused a storm of protest. Was it a real crisis or a storm in a teacup?

match.why: Heat stands for anger and strong emotion.

match.r: a person or thing that brings happiness
match.why: Sunshine is happiness; one ray can brighten a dark day.
A cool head is controlled, not hot with panic or anger.
Turning a cold shoulder to someone shows you don't want contact.
After a storm the air feels fresh; honest talk does the same.

pick.q: In a crisis you want a ___ pilot, not a nervous one.
pick.why: Cool-headed: calm and in control under pressure.

pick.q: Your postcard was ___ during a very grey week in hospital.
pick.why: A ray of sunshine: something that brings happiness in a hard time.

pick.q: The refugee family received ___ from the small Manitoba town that sponsored them.
pick.why: A warm welcome: a friendly, generous greeting.

pick.q: The bride's brother joked that she might ___, but she walked down the aisle smiling.
pick.why: Get cold feet: lose your nerve, classically before a wedding.

pick.q: The committee meeting turned into ___ about funding, with members talking over each other.
pick.why: A heated debate: an angry, emotional argument.

pick.q: I'd planned to unveil the new design myself, but my manager ___ by posting it online first.
pick.why: Stole my thunder: took the attention I expected to get.

spot.q: After the scandal, the senator got a frozen reception at the party conference.
spot.why: The usual collocation is a frosty (or chilly, icy) reception.

spot.q: My boss is wonderfully hot-headed in emergencies; nothing ever rattles her.
spot.why: Hot-headed means quick to anger. Someone calm in a crisis is cool-headed.

spot.q: Our new receptionist is a beam of sunshine, and clients love her.
spot.why: The fixed phrase is a ray of sunshine.

spot.q: Can I take a rain ticket on lunch? I'm stuck in meetings all day.
spot.why: Take a rain check is fixed, even though it came from baseball tickets.

type.q: The argument over parking spaces was a storm in a ___; by Friday nobody cared.
type.why: A storm in a teacup: a fuss about something small.

type.q: He gave his ex the cold ___ at the reunion and spoke only to her friends.
type.why: Give someone the cold shoulder: deliberately ignore them.

type.q: Mum has been a bit under the ___ since her long flight home.
I really wanted to announce the news myself, but she stole my ___.
type.why: Steal someone's thunder: take their moment of attention.

type.q: Volunteers at the airport gave the arriving families a ___ welcome with signs and flowers.
type.why: A warm welcome: warmth means friendliness.

type.q: Every group project needs one ___-headed person who stays calm when deadlines slip.
type.why: Cool-headed, level-headed and clear-headed all mean calm and sensible.

bank.q: The comedian opened the conference with a self-deprecating story to ___.
bank.why: Break the ice: relax a room of strangers.

bank.q: The minister's speech on taxes received ___ from business leaders.
bank.why: A frosty reception: a cold, unfriendly response.

bank.q: Investors ___ when the start-up's losses were published and pulled their money out.
bank.why: Got cold feet: became nervous and backed out.

bank.q: Don't panic about one bad online review; it's ___.
bank.why: A storm in a teacup: a minor issue causing too much worry.

bank.q: My daughter's laugh is ___ on a dull winter evening.
bank.why: A ray of sunshine: something that brings joy.

bank.q: In retail, the week before Black Friday is ___.
bank.why: The calm before the storm: a quiet spell before a very busy time.

bank.q: I'm going to ___ on the hike; my knee is still sore.
bank.why: Take a rain check: decline now, maybe join another time.

bank.q: The council session turned into ___ when the bike lane plan came up.
bank.why: A heated debate: an angry, emotional argument.

bank.q: We need someone cool-___ to handle the media during the crisis.
bank.why: Cool-headed: calm and rational under pressure.

bank.q: Sam was supposed to propose on holiday but got cold ___ at the last minute.
bank.why: Get cold feet: lose your nerve before a commitment.

bank.q: Our guide broke the ___ by teaching us a few words of Icelandic.
bank.why: Break the ice: make strangers feel more relaxed.

bank.q: At my birthday dinner, my little brother stole my ___ by announcing he'd got into medical school.
bank.why: Steal someone's thunder: take attention that was meant for them.

bank.q: I'll take a rain ___ on coffee; my train is delayed.
bank.why: Take a rain check: postpone an invitation politely.

bank.q: She's been under the whether all week with a nasty cold.
bank.why: Weather (rain, sun) not whether (if). Under the weather means slightly ill.

bank.q: The town hall meeting was a hot debate that lasted past midnight.
bank.why: The collocation is a heated debate, not a hot one.

bank.q: The hotel staff gave us a warm welcome even though we arrived at three in the morning.
bank.why: Correct: a warm welcome is the natural phrase for a friendly greeting.

bank.q: My grandmother has always been a ray of sunlight for the whole family.
bank.why: The idiom for a person who brings happiness is a ray of sunshine.

bank.a: She got cold feet the night before the wedding.
alt: The night before the wedding she got cold feet.
bank.why: Get cold feet + time phrase: the night before the wedding.

bank.a: The new tax got a frosty reception from voters.
bank.why: Get a frosty reception from someone: be received coldly.

bank.a: Can I take a rain check on dinner tonight?
bank.why: Take a rain check on + the invitation: a casual way to postpone.
